analysis.title: "Witching Hour": Goldman's Flow Desk Sees Technical Tide Turning As Buybacks, Retail And Foreigners All Line Up For Year-End
key_insights: Goldman's Flow of Funds note "Witching Hour" (Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett, Lee Coppersmith) says the technical setup for US equities is changing even though sentiment is depressed and the macro has no clear path to resolution.

Corporate buybacks went dark in the pre-earnings blackout, with desk flows at 0.8x last year's pace. Goldman expects companies to exit blackout 1-2 days after reporting, so about 10% of the S&P is in an open window by the end of this week and 48% by the end of October.
November is the second-busiest month for corporate repurchases on Goldman's desk, at 10.1% of annual buyback spend, behind only August.
Buyback dispersion: info tech is 46% of executions and down 40% y/y, financials are up 88%, energy up 480% and utilities up 538% (together about 6% of the total).

678 active funds ($2.306T in assets) and 81 passive funds ($1.736T) have an October 31 fiscal year-end, equal to 23% of active fund assets. Goldman calls this the "spooky selling season": tax-motivated selling in laggards fades and some YTD winners slow into month-end, and the supply ends when the calendar flips.
October is the third-largest month for equity mutual fund and ETF outflows, but November and December bring back-to-back inflows that only February-March rivals.

Global equity funds took in $12B in the week to October 7 (vs $16B the prior week), led by tech funds and then utilities. Brazil was the EM standout after its first-round election, and EWZ traded about $8B in one day.

Money market funds took in $166.37B in the week ending October 7, after $15.9B of cumulative outflows over the prior four weeks. That is 1.49% of money fund AUM in one week vs a 4-week average of -0.03%. Cash on the sidelines historically gets deployed in Nov-Dec.

Goldman's Sentiment Indicator (institutional, retail and foreign positioning) is -1.3. Readings between -1 and -1.5 have historically been followed by an average one-month forward return of +2%, which Goldman calls a "moderate tailwind".
CFTC futures positioning is near the 95th percentile, active equity fund flows are in the single digits and the composite indicator is near the 10th percentile.

Foreigners own 18% of the US equity market vs 2% for hedge funds, and their positioning has sat just below the 50th percentile since 2009. Historically midterms trigger foreign buying of about 1.75% of AUM in the six months after the vote (10-episode average since 1986). The article's own arithmetic, on a market above $60T, puts that at roughly $190B.
Citadel's Scott Rubner also flipped bullish on the view that "the buyers are coming back".

Hedge fund info tech exposure is 21.5% gross and 20.4% net (87th/83rd percentile over one year, 97th/80th over five years). Tech was the most net sold US sector last week (-1.0 SD) after being the most net bought in four of the prior five weeks. Funds net bought industrials at the fastest pace since early January (+1.8 SD).

US long/short gross leverage rose 3.8 points to 213% (53rd percentile) while net leverage rose 0.5 points to 46.9% (2nd percentile). The fundamental long/short ratio is 1.565, in the 1st percentile over five years. Goldman's read is that funds own plenty of the AI trade with little net exposure behind it, which tends to produce violent rotations rather than outright crashes.

A Bloomberg study cited by Goldman covers 13 episodes since 1995 where the 10 largest S&P names beat the equal-weight index by more than 8% over three months. The median S&P return afterwards was +10.1% over 6 months and +19.6% over 12 months, vs historical medians of +6.9% and +15%.

CTA tail scenarios into early November: a 2-sigma bond rally brings about $37B of CTA buying, a 2-sigma bond selloff about $23B, a 2-sigma S&P rally only $5.5B, and a 2-sigma S&P drop about $45B of selling. The S&P asymmetry is "firmly to the downside".

CTAs sold roughly $81B of global equities over the past month. US equity positioning is in the 27th percentile (one-year) and 54th (five-year). Goldman's model has CTAs about $40B long the S&P and $6.6B short the Russell 2000, the shortest in the Russell since 2023.
Midterm vol pattern since 2000: SPX and NDX vol see an immediate crush after the vote, then churn lower into year-end. Russell vol held up better and the NDX-SPX vol spread stayed sticky.

SPX 1-month implied vol is near 12 vs a historical midterm average of about 19-20 at the same point, and NDX is about 17-18 vs mid-20s. The article reads this as the post-election crush having already happened about two months early.

A sustained drop in the vol regime would unlock systematic demand that could "help fuel a potential Santa Rally". Options imply historically small daily moves, which Goldman reads as low conviction and "mispriced tails". Goldman's advice is to own gamma ahead of earnings, the midterms and the Fed.

Dissent inside Goldman: Louis Miller (head of equity custom baskets) said on October 4 that "midterms beckon and the result probably won't be risk positive" and still likes owning AI over the ex-AI basket (SPXXAI), the opposite of the flow desk's SPXXAI-over-SPX broadening trade.

BofA's Michael Hartnett sees a Republican Senate with a Democratic House as "Gridlock = Goldilocks" (stocks up more than 5%) and a Democratic sweep as stocks down about 10%. Prediction markets price roughly 65% odds of a sweep. Hartnett also thinks "the most bullish thing the Fed can do now is hike".
Nomura's Charlie McElligott found index vol at the 2nd percentile and implied correlation at the 1.8th percentile, concluding the market's "only fear is of the right-tail".
The article's conclusion is that flows likely carry stocks into December, with the open question being what they are buying.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's flow desk expects the post-midterm foreign bid (about 1.75% of AUM over six months), the end of mutual fund supply on Halloween, reopening buyback windows and November-December retail inflows to carry stocks into year-end. Hartnett sees stocks up more than 5% on a split Congress.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman's Louis Miller says the midterm result "probably won't be risk positive". Hartnett sees stocks down about 10% in a Democratic sweep, which prediction markets price at roughly 65%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Democratic sweep (about 65% odds in prediction markets) that produces a policy shock the foreign bid has to absorb first.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's flow desk likes the ex-AI S&P basket (SPXXAI) vs the S&P or equal-weight as a broadening trade.
tension_points.bear_case: Louis Miller says owning AI over the ex-AI basket "has worked well, and we still like it".

tension_points.bull_case: CTAs still have room to buy: US equity positioning is in the 27th percentile (one-year) after $81B of selling, and the Russell is the shortest since 2023.
tension_points.bear_case: CTA flow asymmetry is "firmly to the downside": about $45B of selling on a 2-sigma S&P drop vs $5.5B of buying on a 2-sigma rally.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 2-sigma drop in the S&P would trigger about $45B of CTA selling.
